title_en: Competition for degree apprenticeships quadruples as university costs rise
title_zh: 大学费用上涨，学位学徒制申请竞争激增至四倍
summary_zh: 英国广播公司获得的信息自由数据显示，当前学年英国每11.3名申请者竞争一个6级学位学徒名额，而2023-24学年为2.8人。随着大学学费随通胀上涨，学生、企业和政府都面临压力：学生申请竞争加剧，企业担心招聘成本与培训内容灵活性，政府则表示将提供招聘激励和免费培训。
reading_passage:
Last month, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he wanted to ensure teenagers had technical routes into careers that could rival the path of a traditional university degree.

His comments came as concerns grow about the immediate and long-term costs of university, with more students wanting to stay at home home rather than moving away, to save money and calls to reform student loan repayments. The cost of undergraduate tuition fees in England is now set to rise every year with inflation.

Degree apprenticeships might look to some like an attractive alternative, but the Freedom of Information data obtained by the BBC suggests they are hard to come by.

There were 11.3 applications for every Level 6 apprenticeship position in the current academic year, compared to 2.8 in 2023-24.

There are similar trends across all apprenticeships at Levels 4, 5 and 6, where there have been 10.6 applications per position - up from 3.6.

Level 4, 5 and 6 qualifications are equivalent to the first, second and third years of an undergraduate degree.

The data only relates to apprenticeships advertised through the Find An Apprenticeship website in England, which is run by the government and subject to Freedom of Information requests. Employers also advertise positions themselves and through other platforms.

Oliver Sidwell, director of Higherin, one of those platforms, said searches for degree apprenticeships had risen by more than 80% this year. He said employers were advertising more degree apprenticeships through his service, but demand was growing faster.

Kieran McRae, 22, applied for a degree apprenticeship but was "devastated" to miss out on a place.

Instead, he studied computer science at the University of Birmingham alongside apprentices who secured a place on the same programme he was rejected from.

"We all went to the same lectures and we had the same labs, the same tutorials," he said.

"[There] was, I think, always a bit of jealousy. Not to say that I wasn't happy for them... but I knew that I was not getting that same free degree or the same salary."

Kieran said he is now happy with the route he took, especially since there were opportunities for industry experience during his course - something the University of Birmingham said had become increasingly important to offer when apprenticeships were so competitive.

But he added: "If I was 18 and offered the degree apprenticeship, 100% I would have taken it."

Kieran McRae shared lecture halls with apprentices on the programme he was rejected from

Anna Helder, 18, applied for 35 apprenticeships while studying at Hereford Sixth Form College and was "ecstatic" when she landed a project management role in London.

"I found it overwhelming the amount of stages that you have to go through," she said.

"You could go two months with zero contact from the company and then suddenly just an email saying: 'You've got an assessment centre next week.'"

Anna applied for 35 apprenticeships before landing a project management role in London

Daniel Edwards, 21, applied for 11 apprenticeships before securing an engineering degree apprenticeship.

Like Anna, he applied to university through Ucas as a "backup".

"University was more straightforward. It's one personal statement that you put out to all universities," he said.

"Your degree apprenticeship... you've got a cover letter, a CV. It's like applying for a real job. You've really got to convey your passion for that specific company."

Daniel said the application process for a degree apprenticeship was similar to a "real job"

Vicky Orsmond advises students at Hereford Sixth Form College about careers and said there was "significant concern" around the cost of going to university, which had sparked interest in degree apprenticeships.

But she said it was not easy for her students, who are competing for relatively few positions outside of the South East - often against more experienced candidates.

"We have lessons where we say to them, 'It's more competitive than many, many university degrees,'" she said.

Vicky said students often find themselves up against more experienced candidates

Businesses say a range of factors put them off hiring apprentices.

Hannah Larsen, policy officer at the British Chambers of Commerce, said demand for degree apprenticeship was rising "at a time when businesses' operating margins are under increasing pressure".

"Higher employment costs, alongside wider economic uncertainty, mean recruitment is being paused, with younger and less experienced workers hit hardest," she said.

She added that there was "considerable uncertainty over the future of apprenticeship funding".

Everything you need to know about university costs

How student loans work for tuition fees and living costs

How do I apply for an apprenticeship and what will I get paid?

At Yorkshire-based manufacturing company Fives, most apprentices are at lower levels and study at nearby Keighley College, but there is one degree apprentice.

Jo Jackson, head of human resources, said she would like to hire more apprentices but training is expensive and the content apprentices are taught is not always "flexible enough".

"Business needs are changing all the time, but it's very, very difficult to change the syllabus," she said.

"If we think about AI and how it's changing the world of work, the apprenticeships don't cover that.

"They can't change quickly enough to keep up."

Competition for some applicants is steeper than others, according to Stephen Evans, chief executive at Learning and Work Institute, who says you are "less likely to get one if you're from a working-class family".

A DWP spokeswoman said the government was introducing a bursary for apprentices whose families receive Universal Credit.

Commenting on the rise in demand more generally, she added: "We're backing employers who take on young apprentices, including hiring incentives worth up to £8,000, and making apprenticeship training completely free for businesses for eligible young people aged 16 to 24."

vocabulary.example: She secured a degree apprenticeship with a large engineering firm.
Completing a vocational qualification can offer an alternative route into nursing.
Demand for skilled workers has increased sharply in the technology sector.

vocabulary.meaning_zh: 竞争激烈的；有竞争力的
vocabulary.example: Graduate schemes are highly competitive, with hundreds of applicants for each vacancy.
Many students take out loans to cover tuition fees.

vocabulary.meaning_zh: 营业利润率；营业利润空间
vocabulary.example: Rising energy costs have squeezed operating margins across the manufacturing industry.

vocabulary.meaning_zh: 评估中心（招聘筛选环节）
vocabulary.example: Applicants must attend an assessment centre as part of the selection process.
The long application process put off many potential candidates.
The company plans to take on ten new trainees this year.

difficult_sentences.sentence: His comments came as concerns grow about the immediate and long-term costs of university, with more students wanting to stay at home home rather than moving away, to save money and calls to reform student loan repayments.
difficult_sentences.explanation_zh: 主句为 `His comments came`，`as` 引导时间状语从句表示“随着……”，`with` 介词短语补充说明同时出现的两个因素：一是更多学生希望留在家中而非搬走，二是要求改革学生贷款偿还制度的呼声。句中 `to save money` 为目的状语，说明学生留在家中的原因。
difficult_sentences.grammar_point: `as` 表伴随的时间状语从句；`with` + 名词/动名词短语引出伴随情况；不定式 `to save money` 作目的状语
difficult_sentences.translation_zh: 他发表上述言论之际，人们对大学短期和长期费用的担忧日益加剧，更多学生希望留在家中而不是搬走以节省开支，同时要求改革学生贷款偿还制度的呼声也在出现。

difficult_sentences.sentence: Degree apprenticeships might look to some like an attractive alternative, but the Freedom of Information data obtained by the BBC suggests they are hard to come by.
difficult_sentences.explanation_zh: 本句为 `but` 连接的并列句。前一分句说明学位学徒制可能看起来像有吸引力的替代选择，其中 `might look` 是情态动词表示不确定判断；后一分句用 `obtained by the BBC` 作后置定语修饰 `data`，`suggests` 后接省略 `that` 的宾语从句 `they are hard to come by`，形成转折关系。
difficult_sentences.grammar_point: `might look` 表不确定；过去分词短语 `obtained by...` 作后置定语；`suggests` 后省略 `that` 的宾语从句
difficult_sentences.translation_zh: 学位学徒制在一些人看来或许是有吸引力的替代方案，但BBC获得的信息自由数据显示，这类机会难以获得。

difficult_sentences.sentence: Not to say that I wasn't happy for them... but I knew that I was not getting that same free degree or the same salary.
difficult_sentences.explanation_zh: 该句以 `Not to say that` 开头，表示“这并不是说……”，用于先否定一种误解，再引出真实感受。主句为 `but` 后的 `I knew that...`，其中 `that` 引导宾语从句，说明他深知自己没有获得同样免费的学位或同样的薪水。
difficult_sentences.grammar_point: `not to say that` 作让步性插入语；`but` 转折；`that` 引导宾语从句；`same...or...` 并列结构
difficult_sentences.translation_zh: 这并不是说我不为他们感到高兴……但我知道我没有获得同样免费的学位或同样的薪水。

difficult_sentences.sentence: But she said it was not easy for her students, who are competing for relatively few positions outside of the South East - often against more experienced candidates.
difficult_sentences.explanation_zh: 主句为 `But she said it was not easy for her students`，其中 `it` 为形式主语，真正主语是 `for her students` 的不定式逻辑主语；`who` 引导非限制性定语从句，补充说明学生们在东南部以外竞争相对较少的职位；破折号后的 `often against more experienced candidates` 进一步说明他们还要面对经验更丰富的候选人。
difficult_sentences.grammar_point: `it` 作形式主语的主语从句；`who` 引导非限制性定语从句；破折号用于补充说明
difficult_sentences.translation_zh: 但她说，这对她的学生来说并不容易，他们要在东南部以外竞争相对较少的职位——而且往往还要面对经验更丰富的候选人。

idioms.usage_note: 常用于机会、工作、住房等名词之后，表示供应稀缺；多用于新闻报道和书面语。
idioms.example: Affordable housing in the city centre is hard to come by.

idioms.usage_note: 非正式，后接名词或动名词，常表示遇到强劲对手或困难。
idioms.example: New graduates are often up against more experienced candidates.

idioms.usage_note: 非正式，后接名词或动名词，常表示因未参与而失去好处。
idioms.example: He missed out on a place on the graduate scheme.

idioms.meaning_zh: 受到最严重打击；受影响最大
idioms.usage_note: 被动用法，常与 `economy`、`workers`、`families` 等词连用，多见于经济类新闻。
idioms.example: Small businesses were hit hardest by the rise in energy prices.

idioms.usage_note: 不及物，常与 `with` 连用，表示跟上变化、进度或他人。
idioms.example: Apprenticeship syllabuses often struggle to keep up with technological change.

reading_questions.question: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the article?

options.A: University tuition fees in England are falling, leading to a decline in degree apprenticeship applications.
options.B: Degree apprenticeships are now more widely available than full-time undergraduate degrees.
options.C: Employers are reducing degree apprenticeship places because training is too expensive and inflexible.
options.D: Although degree apprenticeships appeal to students as a cheaper option, competition for them has intensified sharply.

reading_questions.question: According to the Freedom of Information data obtained by the BBC, how did applications per Level 6 apprenticeship position change?

options.A: They rose from 3.6 to 10.6 for Level 4 positions.
options.B: They fell from 11.3 in 2023-24 to 2.8 in the current year.
options.C: They remained unchanged at 2.8 applications per position.
options.D: They rose from 2.8 in 2023-24 to 11.3 in the current year.

reading_questions.question: What can be inferred from Kieran McRae's experience?

options.A: Kieran regretted not taking a different degree because he was unhappy with the university's industry experience opportunities.
options.B: University students and degree apprentices on the same programme can take identical lectures and labs, but only apprentices receive a salary and free degree.
options.C: Degree apprentices are usually required to attend fewer lectures than full-time students.
options.D: Kieran was not happy for the apprentices who secured places because he thought the selection process was unfair.

reading_questions.question: In paragraph 2, the word 'reform' is closest in meaning to which of the following?
Which of the following best describes the author's tone when discussing the data on degree apprenticeship competition?

options.A: Cautious, because the figures only cover one government-run website and may not include all advertised apprenticeships.
options.B: Outraged, because the government has failed to provide enough apprenticeship places.
options.C: Celebratory, because more students are choosing vocational routes.
options.D: Sceptical that degree apprenticeships are worth pursuing at all.

reading_questions.question: How does the author organise the passage?

options.A: By starting with student personal stories, then moving to general statistics, and finally proposing one solution.
options.B: By comparing degree apprenticeships with university education throughout and ending with a list of future policy changes.
options.C: By opening with a political statement, then presenting data, student and employer experiences, and a government response.
options.D: By outlining historical trends in university tuition fees before analysing regional differences in apprenticeship availability.

reading_questions.question: Which title best fits the article?

options.A: Competition for Degree Apprenticeships Soars as University Costs Rise
options.B: Government Expands Free Apprenticeship Training for All Ages
options.C: Employers Abandon Apprenticeships Because of Rising Operating Costs
options.D: Prime Minister Urges All Teenagers to Choose Technical Routes

sources.title: Competition for degree apprenticeships quadruples as university costs rise
